name: introduction_1
content: This wave climate report presents wave information for {locName} in {cntName}. It provides an overview of wind-generated surface gravity waves, commonly referred to as wind waves and swell. The wave climate is defined here as the statistical characterization of wave conditions over a {hindcastDuration}-year period. The report describes the average wave conditions (Page X), the variability of wave conditions (Page X), and severe and extreme wave events (Page X). Comparable wave climate reports are available for more than 200 locations across the Pacific, including major ports, populated areas, tide gauge sites, and other regions of particular interest. Other locations within {cntName} are shown in Figure 1 (Front Page). Given the limited availability of in situ wave observations across the Pacific, the information presented here has been derived from a numerical regional wave hindcast.

name: introduction_2
content: The wave hindcast evaluated wave conditions in the region between {yearStart} and {yearEnd}. It was originally produced by the Centre for Australian Weather and Climate Research and has been updated by the Bureau of Meteorology (Australia) since 2013. The hindcast focuses on the central and South Pacific, with a spatial resolution ranging from 10 to 4 arcminutes (~20 to 8 km), providing reliable estimates of offshore wave conditions. The model was constrained using the best available data and validated against wave measurements. In the Pacific region, the hindcast achieved reasonably good results, with an average skill score of 0.85 (scores between 0.8 and 0.9 are considered good, and scores above 0.9 are considered excellent; see Table 1). For more information on the regional wave hindcast, readers are referred to Durrant et al. (2014) and Smith et al. (2020). This report was generated by a computer program developed at SPC-Geoscience, which analysed the output from the wave hindcast and summarised the findings. Despite best efforts to ensure accuracy, this report may contain errors or omissions and should be used with caution.

name: averageWaveConditions_1
content: Wave conditions are generally described by the significant wave height, the peak period, and the peak direction. The significant wave height is defined as the average height (from trough to crest) of the highest one-third of waves and corresponds to the wave height that would typically be reported by an experienced observer. The peak period represents the time interval between successive waves within the dominant wave system, while the peak direction indicates the direction from which these dominant waves originate. Note that this document follows the nautical convention, meaning that wave (and wind) directions are reported as the direction they are coming from, measured clockwise from geographic North.

name: averageWaveConditions_2
content: This page provides information on the average wave climate of {locName} in {cntName}. The average sea state is {avgWave_seaState} and is dominated by {avgWave_waveType}. The annual mean wave height is {avgWave_meanHs:.2f} meters, the annual mean wave direction is {avgWave_meanDp:.0f}°, and the annual mean wave period is {avgWave_meanTp:.2f} seconds. Table 2 summarises the mean wave conditions for {locName}.

name: averageWaveConditions_3
content: In the Pacific, waves often arrive from multiple directions and periods. At {locName}, there are typically more than {avgWave_nComponents:.0f} distinct wave components. Wave conditions are generally stable over a few hours. Mean annual and seasonal variability is reported in Table 2. For more details, see Page X.

name: meanWaveRose_1
content: The mean wave conditions do not capture the full range of wave heights and directions at {locName}. The wave rose (Figure 2) provides a better representation, showing typical wave directions and associated heights. Circles (polar axis) indicate frequency of occurrence, with each circle representing 10%, wedges cover 20 degrees direction ranges. Wave heights are grouped in 0.25 m intervals, each represented by a colour on the scale to the right of the rose.

name: meanWaveRose_2
content: {meanWaRose_waveHistory} {meanWaRose_seaState} Waves principaly came from the {meanWaRose_Dirp}.

name: waveVariation_1
content: The wave climate varies throughout the year due to seasonal changes in Pacific wind patterns. This page summarizes these variations for {locName}. Monthly variability, measured as the coefficient of variation of wave height, is {waveVar_HsVarCoeff:.1f}%. Locations exposed mainly to trade winds typically show the smallest variation (<25%), Southern Ocean swell-exposed sites show 25 to 30%, and North Pacific swell-exposed sites show over 30%. Monthly variability indicates month-to-month changes, while seasonal wave roses (Figure 3) provide a clearer picture of seasonal patterns.

name: waveVariation_2
content: {waveVar_summerSeaState} The principal wave direction is from the {waveVar_summerDirp}. {waveVar_autumnSeaState} The principal wave direction is from the {waveVar_autumnDirp}. {waveVar_winterSeaState} The principal wave direction is from the {waveVar_winterDirp}. {waveVar_springSeaState} The principal wave direction is from the {waveVar_springDirp}.

name: waveVariation_3
content: Monthly wave height, period, and direction illustrate seasonal changes in wave conditions, highlighting transitions between seasons. The average wave height during calm periods (lowest 10%) and large swell events (highest 10%) also varies seasonally. Figure 4 can assist in identifying the most suitable months for servicing or installing offshore structures and moorings.

name: waveVariation_4
content: Waves vary not only seasonally but also from year to year due to climate oscillations. These inter-annual changes are generally smaller than seasonal variations but can be significant during events such as El Niño. At {locName}, the inter-annual variability of wave height (coefficient of variation) is {waveVar_HsVarCoeff_InterAnnual:.1f}%, compared with an average of 7% across the Pacific. Since 1979, the mean annual wave height at {locName} has {waveVar_HsTrend}, and the mean annual wave height is {waveVar_CorrClimate}. The 1997/1998 El Niño had a major impact on the Pacific wave climate, causing dramatic changes in wave patterns across most islands (Figure 5).

name: largeSevereWaves_1
content: From time to time, waves increase in size to the point where they can cause beach erosion or coastal inundation. Large waves are defined as those exceeding the 90th percentile of wave height, meaning they occur approximately 10% of the time (around 37 days per year). They typically represent the largest events expected each month. While large waves rarely cause coastal damage on their own, they can create hazardous conditions for water activities. Coastal inundation and erosion are more likely when large waves coincide with high spring tides, such as perigean spring tides (king tides). At {locName}, the threshold for large waves is {severeWave_thresholdLarge:.2f} meters.

name: largeSevereWaves_2
content: Severe waves are less frequent than large waves, occurring less than 1% of the time (about 4 days per year) and typically once or twice annually. They can cause coastal erosion and inundation, particularly when coinciding with spring tides, and create hazardous conditions for water activities. At {locName}, the threshold for severe waves is {severeWave_thresholdSevere:.2f} meters.

name: largeSevereWaves_3
content: Large and severe waves can be generated by various weather events, including cyclones, distant extratropical storms, and fresh trade winds. The direction and period of these waves indicate their origin. This information can be observed in the large, severe, and extreme wave rose (Figure 6). At {locName}, the dominant direction for waves exceeding {severeWave_thresholdLarge:.2f} meters is from the {severeWave_Dirp}.

name: largeSevereWaves_4
content: Larger waves can be generated by various meteorological phenomena, such as tropical cyclones, extratropical storms, or fresh trade wind events. These events are highly seasonal, and so are the large waves. At {locName}, large waves are typically highest in {severeWave_mainSeason}, although they can occur during other seasons. The monthly variability of the large wave threshold (90th percentile) at {locName} is {severeWave_monthlyVarCoeff:.2f}% (Figure 7). As mean wave height varies from year to year, so do the large waves; the annual variability of the large wave threshold at {locName} is {severeWave_yearlyVarCoeff:.2f}% (Figure 8).

name: extremeWaves_1
content: A list of the 30 largest wave events is presented in Table 3, showing their ranking, date, wave height, wave period, and direction at the event peak. The largest event at {locName} since {yearStart} occurred on {extremeWave_largestDate}, exceeding {extremeWave_largestHs:.0f} meters, which is considered {extremeWave_largestCondition}. All listed events have wave heights above {extremeWave_smallestHs:.0f} meters, considered {extremeWave_smallestCondition}. This list can be used to estimate the probability of occurrence of waves larger than the average largest annual wave height, an analysis known as extreme wave analysis, presented on the next page.

name: extremeWaves_2
content: Extreme waves analysis is used to assess the probability of wave events exceeding the severe wave height. They are often applied to evaluate community vulnerability to coastal inundation and to determine the design height of structures such as seawalls or jetties. Extreme wave analysis is a statistical approach that examines the distribution of past wave events and extrapolates the likelihood of unusually large events that may not have been observed. This probability is commonly expressed as the Annual Return Interval (ARI), which represents the chance of an event occurring within a given year. For example, a 100-year ARI event has a 1% probability of occurring in any year, while a 50-year ARI event has a 2% probability.

name: extremeWaves_3
content: The analysis for {locName} was conducted by defining a severe wave height threshold and fitting a Generalised Pareto Distribution (GPD). The optimum threshold was {extremeWave_EVA_threshold:.2f} meters. Over the {hindcastDuration}-year wave hindcast, {extremeWave_EVA_nEvents} wave events reached or exceeded this threshold. The GPD was fitted to the maximum wave height of each event (Figure 9). While extreme wave analyses are valuable tools, they are sensitive to data availability, the type of distribution used, and the selected threshold, and may not fully capture waves generated by tropical cyclones. More detailed analyses are required for applications such as coastal infrastructure design and coastal hazard planning.

name: wind_1
content: Wind drives all waves, and local winds can significantly influence local wave conditions. At {locName}, the prevailing wind is dominated by {wind_tradeWinds}, with a mean speed of {wind_wSpeed:.2f} m/s ({wind_wSpeedKnots:.2f} knots) from the {wind_Dirp}. Figure 11 shows the wind rose, and Figure 12 shows monthly mean wind speed and direction. Directions follow the nautical convention, indicating where the wind is coming from.
